after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4-{e}^{3x} & >2 \\ -{e}^{3x} & >6 \\ {e}^{3x} & <-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $e>0,$ we have

$$
{e}^{3x}>0
$$

for every real value of $x.$

Therefore, ${e}^{3x}$ cannot be less than $-6.$ Hence, the inequality

$$
{e}^{3x}<-6
$$

has no solutions.

Question 3
?

Solve the inequality 7⋅41−x<3x.

a
x>ln⁡4+ln⁡7ln⁡3+ln⁡4
b
 x>ln⁡3+ln⁡7ln⁡6+ln⁡7
c
 x<ln⁡3+ln⁡7ln⁡4+ln⁡7
d
 x>ln⁡3+ln⁡7ln⁡4+ln⁡7
e
 x<ln⁡4+ln⁡7ln⁡3+ln⁡4
Submit

decision.explanation: Multiplying by 4^x gives 28<12^x. Taking natural logarithms and dividing by ln(12)>0 yields x>ln(28)/ln(12)=(ln(4)+ln(7))/(ln(3)+ln(4)).

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\cdot {4}^{1-x} & <{3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(7\cdot {4}^{1-x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡7+(1-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡7+\operatorname{ln}⁡4-x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡4+\operatorname{ln}⁡7 & <x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\ x & >\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4+\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

a

c

Submit

EXPLANATION

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

7⋅41−x<3xln⁡(7⋅41−x)<ln⁡(3x)ln⁡7+(1−x)ln⁡4<xln⁡3ln⁡7+ln⁡4−xln⁡4<xln⁡3ln⁡4+ln⁡7<x(ln⁡3+ln⁡4)x>ln⁡4+ln⁡7ln⁡3+ln⁡4

content.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\cdot {4}^{1-x} & <{3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(7\cdot {4}^{1-x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡7+(1-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡7+\operatorname{ln}⁡4-x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡4+\operatorname{ln}⁡7 & <x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\ x & >\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4+\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{(0.62)}^{x+5}\le 1 \\ {(0.62)}^{x+5}\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[(0.62)^{x+5}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ (x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡0.62 & \le 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡0.62$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & \ge \frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡0.62} \\ x & \ge \frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡0.62}-5\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Multiplying by 3 gives (1/2)^{x+1}≤1/3. Taking logarithms yields -(x+1)ln(2)≤-ln(3), so x+1≥ln(3)/ln(2). Thus x≥ln(3)/ln(2)-1.

after.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{9} \\ {(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ (x+1)(-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le -\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & \ge \frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x & \ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{9} \\ {(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ (x+1)(-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le -\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & \ge \frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x & \ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1\end{aligned}
$$
